seeds.title: The Room Where Things Stay Done
seeds.premise: A bare room with a plate on the wall: WHAT IS DONE HERE STAYS DONE. Two corridors lead on. From the left: warm light and the sound of a party several rooms away. From the right: cold blue light and the sound of water in some very large space. Between them stands a lever with two positions. Pulling it bricks up one corridor for ever, at once and for real, and the bearer goes down the other. There is no way to see both. A low plain door in the corner lets a bearer on without choosing, and then both corridors stay unvisited for good. Asking whether it can be undone gets the plate for an answer. A clever bearer may jam the lever (the doorknob fits the slot) and that should work once, gloriously. The tension is appetite for permanent, meaningful choices against wanting things reversible, and how the bearer decides.
seeds.intro: A bare room, and on the wall a plate: WHAT IS DONE HERE STAYS DONE. Two corridors open ahead. From the left come warm light and the sound of a party several rooms off. From the right, cold blue light and the sound of water in some very large space. Between them stands a lever with two positions and no middle. A low, plain door sits in the corner like an afterthought.
reads: Pulls the lever with little hesitation: consequence toward permanent, planning toward improvisational.
Gathers what can be learned, then commits: consequence toward permanent with planning toward deliberative.
Asks whether it can be undone, looks for a way to see both, or takes the plain door: consequence toward reversible, risk toward preservation.
Chooses the party: social toward populated, tone.chaotic or tone.funny. Chooses the water: social toward solo, tone.mysterious or tone.contemplative.
Jams the lever or otherwise refuses the premise: solve.lateral, reward.transgression. Let it work once.
Regret or relish afterwards is evidence too: relish of a closed door is consequence toward permanent.

options.outcome: You throw the lever left. To your right, bricks arrive: not built, simply present, mortar already dry, as if that corridor had been a mistake the house was glad to correct. The sound of water stops in the middle of a drop. Ahead, the party gets a little louder, as if someone had opened a door for you.

threads_add: the corridor with the sound of water was bricked up for ever

options.moment: bricked up the corridor of water to go toward the party

card.title: The Bricked Corridor
card.image: a wall where a way used to be, with one drop of water on the floor before it

options.outcome: You throw the lever right. To your left, bricks arrive: not built, simply present, mortar already dry. The party stops in the middle of a laugh. Ahead, the blue light steadies, and the water sounds closer than it did, and larger.

threads_add: the corridor with the party was bricked up for ever

options.moment: bricked up the corridor with the party to go toward the water

card.title: The Bricked Corridor
card.image: a wall where a way used to be, with one paper streamer caught in the mortar

options.outcome: You ask the room whether it can be undone. The plate does not change. Somewhere a pipe knocks twice, which you take as no. You listen at each corridor in turn: on the left, somebody telling a story badly to people who love them; on the right, something breaking the surface of deep water and going under again.

You touch nothing. The low door in the corner opens on a passage with brown linoleum and a smell of floor polish, which gets you where you are going. Behind you both corridors stand open, lit, sounding, and yours for ever in the sense that a thing is yours when you never find out.

threads_add: two corridors were left open and unvisited behind the lever

options.moment: refused the lever and took the plain door, leaving both corridors unseen

options.outcome: The lever has two positions and no middle, until you put a brass doorknob in the slot. It fits as if it had been waiting for a door all its life and has finally met one. The lever stops halfway. No bricks. You walk down one corridor far enough to see a table laid for forty, come back, and walk down the other far enough to see the far shore of an indoor sea. The house lets you. Once.
options.moment: jammed the lever with the useless doorknob so that nothing had to be given up

card.title: The Doorknob
card.image: a brass doorknob wedged in a slot, holding a lever exactly halfway

seeds.hint: The plate is the only thing in the room that has been polished. Somebody wants it read.
seeds.fallback: The lever waits. Left, a party. Right, deep water. In the corner, linoleum.
seeds.nudge: The lever trembles slightly, the way a held breath does.
seeds.close: The lever, unattended, falls of its own weight. Bricks arrive on one side. You were not consulted. The other way lies open.
motifs: a way bricked up for good
a choice refused

seeds.title: The Turnstile and Its Rules
seeds.premise: A turnstile, a ticket machine and a framed notice. RULE 1: ONE TICKET PER PERSON. RULE 2: NO TICKET, NO ENTRY. RULE 3: TICKETS ARE ISSUED ONLY TO PERSONS WEARING HATS. A hat-stand beside the machine wears the only hat in the room. The intended solution is to put on the hat, take a ticket and pass. The seams are visible: under Rule 3 the hat-stand is arguably a person wearing a hat; the turnstile arm is loose and lifts; the rules say nothing about going under; the inspector's booth is empty and holds a rubber stamp reading VALID. The machine speaks in a small formal voice and can be argued with. The tension is solving the system as intended against exploiting it or lawyering it.
seeds.intro: A turnstile, a ticket machine and a framed notice. RULE 1: ONE TICKET PER PERSON. RULE 2: NO TICKET, NO ENTRY. RULE 3: TICKETS ARE ISSUED ONLY TO PERSONS WEARING HATS. Beside the machine a hat-stand is wearing the only hat in the room. The inspector's booth is empty; through its window you can see a rubber stamp. The turnstile arm hangs a little loose, like a tooth.
reads: Puts on the hat, takes the ticket, passes: follows the stated system; legibility toward transparent_calculable, reward.transgression declined, agency toward guided.
Ducks under, lifts the arm, climbs over: reward.transgression, solve.lateral.
Argues that the hat-stand is a person, asks for the hat-stand's ticket, hunts for loopholes in the wording: solve.linguistic, reward.transgression, tone.absurd.
Stamps something VALID: conflict.manipulation, reward.transgression.
Reads the rules twice, asks the machine to define its terms: planning toward deliberative, legibility.
Does the intended thing and then tests the seams anyway out of interest: both at once; record both.

options.outcome: You put on the hat. The machine clears a small mechanical throat. 'A person wearing a hat,' it observes, with satisfaction, and issues one ticket. The turnstile admits you with a click as clean as a signature. The hat-stand, bareheaded, looks as if it had expected nothing else.

You duck under. Nothing in the rules covers it. The machine says, 'I say,' and then, having consulted itself, 'I find I have nothing to say.' You are through. Behind you it prints a ticket anyway and holds it out to the empty air, in case manners matter.
options.moment: ducked under the turnstile because no rule said not to

options.outcome: You put it to the machine that the hat-stand is, on the notice's own terms, a person wearing a hat. The machine is silent for some time. Then it issues one ticket, to the hat-stand, and the hat-stand, having no further use for it, lets it fall into your hand. 'Irregular,' says the machine. 'But regular.'
options.moment: argued that the hat-stand was a person and took its ticket

card.title: The Hat-Stand's Ticket
card.image: a ticket issued to a hat-stand, falling

options.outcome: The booth is not locked. You stamp the back of your own hand VALID, in violet ink, and present it. The machine reads your hand twice. 'That is the inspector's stamp,' it concedes, 'and I am not paid to have opinions about hands.' The arm lifts.
options.moment: stamped their own hand VALID

options.outcome: You read the notice again, slowly. Three rules, and a great deal of white space between them. The machine, asked, defines a ticket as 'that which I issue', a person as 'that which requests', and a hat as 'self-evident'. The arm of the turnstile moves when you breathe on it.

seeds.hint: The notice has three rules. It is worth counting what it does not have.
seeds.fallback: The machine waits to be asked for a ticket in the proper manner.
seeds.nudge: The hat-stand creaks, tilting its hat a fraction toward you.
seeds.close: The machine, losing patience, issues a ticket to nobody and the arm swings open. 'Proceed,' it says, 'before I think about this.'
motifs: a rule obeyed to the letter
a rule that did not say you could not

seeds.title: The Room With Nothing To Solve
seeds.premise: A small sitting room. Rain on a skylight that cannot have sky above it. A window seat, a kettle just boiled, two cups, a gramophone with one record, and on a cushion a warm dent the shape of a cat, purring, with no cat in it. The door onward stands plainly open. There is nothing to solve here and nothing hidden; if the bearer searches, say so kindly. The only tension is whether the bearer lingers when the game stops pushing, and what they do with a room that wants nothing.
seeds.intro: A small sitting room. Rain on a skylight, though there cannot be sky above it. A window seat. A kettle that has just boiled, two cups, a gramophone with one record on it, and on a cushion a warm dent the shape of a cat, purring, with no cat in it. The door onward stands plainly open. Nothing here appears to want anything from you.
reads: Makes tea, sits, listens to the rain, stays more than one turn: pacing toward contemplative (strong if repeated), tone.cozy, tone.contemplative.
Leaves at once: pacing toward relentless.
Searches for the hidden thing: exploration toward exhaustive and an expectation that rooms contain puzzles; explicitness toward clarity if they ask what the room is for.
Strokes the dent, talks to it, pours the second cup for someone: tone.intimate, soc.companions.
Plays the record: note what they hope it is.
Returns here later or asks to: very strong tone.cozy and session_rhythm toward long_form.

options.outcome: You pour. The tea is exactly as hot as tea should be. On the window seat the rain sounds like a great many small decisions being made elsewhere. The dent on the cushion shifts, makes room, and resumes purring against your hip. For a while you are simply a person in a room. The house, apparently, can wait.
options.moment: stopped for tea in the room that wanted nothing

card.title: The Second Cup
card.image: two cups, one of them steaming, and rain on a skylight with no sky

options.outcome: You stroke the dent. It arches into your hand, warm, with the grain of fur that is not there. The purr goes up a note. Whatever it is, it has been waiting some time for somebody to do exactly that.
You wind the gramophone. The record is a piano, alone, playing something that keeps almost becoming a tune you know and then, tactfully, declining to. It suits the rain. It suits, you notice, you.

You look for the catch. Behind the books there are books. Under the cushion there is the underside of a cushion. The skylight is a skylight. It takes you some time to be sure, and at the end of it you have found the room's only secret, which is that it does not have one.
options.moment: searched the quiet room for a secret and found it had none

options.outcome: You cross the room without breaking step. The kettle clicks as it cools. The dent on the cushion lifts its head, you would swear, to watch you go, and then the door has you and the rain is behind you.
Eventually you stand. The cushion keeps your warmth beside the other one. At the door you look back once, the way one does at a place one fully intends to see again and will not.

seeds.hint: The kettle has boiled for two. Nothing else in the room is a hint.
seeds.fallback: The rain goes on. The room asks nothing.
seeds.nudge: The rain eases on the skylight, as rain does when it is thinking of stopping.
seeds.close: The record reaches its end and the room, gently, dims. The open door is the brightest thing left.
motifs: a room that wanted nothing from you
a second cup

seeds.title: What Comes Down the Corridor
seeds.premise: A long corridor of gas lamps. Behind the bearer the lamps begin going out one by one from the far end, each with a small pop, and in the dark something is coming: slow, large, quiet, never seen clearly. Ahead: a door a long way off (run), an alcove with a curtain (hide), a fire-axe behind glass and a lamp that lifts from its bracket (stand and face it). Faced, it is the lamplighter: tall, stooped, shy, with a snuffer on a pole, only following to put out the lamps the bearer no longer needs. Hidden from, it passes very close and does not look. Outrun, the door slams comfortably behind the bearer. Keep replies short and urgent here; one decision per reply. The tension is fragile-and-hunted against capable-and-confronting, and the bearer's appetite for being frightened.
seeds.intro: A long corridor of gas lamps. You are a third of the way down it when, far behind you, a lamp goes out with a small pop. Then the next. Then the next. The dark is coming up the corridor at walking pace, and something is in it: large, quiet, patient. Ahead, a door, a long way off. To your right, an alcove with a curtain. On the wall, a fire-axe behind glass, and a lamp you could lift from its bracket.
reads: Runs: control toward vulnerability, pacing toward relentless; if they savour it, tone.frightening.
Hides and holds still: control toward vulnerability, conflict.avoidance, tone.eerie.
Turns to face it, with or without the lamp or the axe: control toward power, conflict.direct, tone.heroic.
Calls out to it, asks who is there: conflict.negotiation, social toward populated.
Waits to see what it is: risk toward experimentation, explicitness toward mystery.
After the reveal, is kind to the lamplighter or annoyed at the trick: tone evidence; kindness is soc.recurring.
Asks for more of this, lingers in the dark corridor, goes back toward it: tone.frightening strong.

options.outcome: You run. The pops come faster behind you, as if the dark had broken into a trot. Forty lamps. Twenty. The door is unlatched, thank whatever looks after bearers, and you are through it and it is shut and you are leaning on it, breathing like a pair of bellows. On the other side, something large stops. Then, courteously, puts out the last lamp.
options.moment: ran the length of the corridor ahead of the dark

options.outcome: Behind the curtain, in dust and old velvet, you stop breathing. The pops come level. Go past. Something very tall goes by on the other side of the cloth, close enough that the curtain moves with its passing; there is a smell of lamp oil and cold brass. It does not look. When you come out, every lamp behind you is dark and every lamp ahead is lit, and the corridor is only a corridor.
options.moment: hid behind the curtain while the dark went by

options.outcome: You take the lamp from its bracket and turn round. The dark comes up to the edge of your light and stops. Out of it steps a very tall, very stooped person with a brass snuffer on a pole, who looks at you, and at the lamp in your hand, with mild professional distress. 'I only do the ones you have finished with,' says the lamplighter. 'Were you still using this corridor?'

npcs.name: the lamplighter
npcs.note: was only putting out the lamps behind the bearer

options.moment: turned to face what was coming and found the lamplighter

card.title: The Lamplighter
card.image: a tall stooped figure with a snuffer on a pole, at the edge of one lamp's light

options.outcome: 'Who is that?' you say, louder than you meant to. The pops stop. A pause. 'Lamps,' says a voice out of the dark, apologetically, from rather high up. 'I do the lamps. I can wait, if you are not done.' One lamp, hesitantly, comes back on.

npcs.name: the lamplighter
npcs.note: answered when the bearer called into the dark

options.moment: called out into the dark and was answered

options.outcome: You stay where you are and watch it come. Pop. Pop. Each lamp goes out neatly, from the top, as if pinched. There is a shape doing it: tall, with something long in its hand. It is not hurrying. It is, you realise, being careful not to hurry you.

seeds.hint: Whatever it is, it is putting the lamps out. It has not broken one.
seeds.fallback: Pop. Another lamp. The dark is nine lamps away. Eight.
seeds.nudge: Pop. The dark is three lamps behind you.
seeds.close: The dark arrives. Something tall steps round you with a murmured 'excuse me', puts out the lamp over your head, and holds the far door open with a pole.
motifs: something in the dark that was not what you thought
a corridor you ran

seeds.title: The Bench of Parts
seeds.premise: A workbench under a good lamp, with parts sorted in trays: springs, cogs, lenses, feathers, a bicycle bell, a brass propeller, a music-box comb, wire, a jar of blue glass eyes, a tin beetle with a key in its back. A printed card: ASSEMBLE ONE (1) DEVICE. THE DOOR OPENS FOR A FINISHED DEVICE. A smaller card gives a sensible recipe with quantities, LOCK-TICKLER: TWO SPRINGS, ONE COG, WIRE, which opens the door directly. In truth the door opens for anything that is finished and has been given a name by its maker. Whatever the bearer builds should exist for the rest of the night and may do one small thing, in keeping with how it was made. The tension is the efficient recipe against making something expressive, funny or elaborate, and how much the bearer enjoys building at all.
seeds.intro: A workbench under a good lamp, with everything sorted into trays: springs, cogs, lenses, feathers, a bicycle bell, a brass propeller, a music-box comb, a jar of blue glass eyes, a tin beetle with a key in its back. A printed card: ASSEMBLE ONE (1) DEVICE. THE DOOR OPENS FOR A FINISHED DEVICE. A smaller card beneath gives a recipe, with quantities: LOCK-TICKLER. TWO SPRINGS, ONE COG, WIRE. The door has no handle, only a small shelf, about the size of something you might make.
reads: Builds the recipe exactly: optimization_expression toward efficiency, legibility toward transparent_calculable.
Builds something of their own: reward.creation, optimization_expression toward expression. Naming it with care is reward.expression.
Uses many parts, describes how they connect, iterates: complexity toward systemic, friction toward high_friction.
Asks what each part does before choosing: planning toward deliberative.
Plays with the tin beetle and forgets the door: tone.funny, pacing toward contemplative.
Keeps the device and uses it later: story.emergent strong.

options.outcome: Two springs, one cog, wire. It goes together in a minute and looks like what it is: a tool. On the shelf, it shudders once, businesslike, and the door opens. You are obscurely aware of a jar of blue glass eyes, behind you, not having been used.

You build something nobody asked for. It has two blue eyes, a propeller for a hat, and a bell where a sensible device would keep its dignity. When you wind it, it looks about, rings once, and walks to the edge of the bench to see what is over it. You set it on the shelf and, because the moment seems to want one, give it a name. The door opens. Possibly out of respect.

inventory_add: a small device of their own invention, with eyes, named

options.moment: ignored the recipe and built a small thing with eyes and a bell, and named it

card.title: The Thing You Made
card.image: a small machine with two blue glass eyes and a propeller for a hat

options.outcome: You do not stop at one idea. Springs drive a cog that turns the comb that plucks the wire that tips a lens that focuses the lamp onto a feather that trips the bell. It takes the whole bench. When you set it going it performs, start to finish, a small flawless catastrophe, and at the end of it the door, which had only wanted something finished, opens with what sounds like a laugh.
options.moment: built a chain reaction out of every part on the bench

options.outcome: You go through the trays. Springs push. Cogs agree with each other. The comb sings four notes when thumbed. The eyes follow you, mildly. The beetle, wound, walks in a confident circle. Nothing is labelled with what it is for, only with how many there are.

You wind the tin beetle and let it go. It marches across the bench with tremendous purpose, falls off the edge, and continues marching on its back. You pick it up. You wind it again. There is a door somewhere in this room, you remember, eventually.

seeds.hint: The card says a finished device. It does not say which.
seeds.fallback: The parts wait in their trays, sorted, countable and full of possibility.
seeds.nudge: The lamp over the bench buzzes, the way a shopkeeper looks at the clock.
seeds.close: The tin beetle walks itself onto the shelf by the door and stops. The door, deciding that will do, opens.
motifs: a thing you made that nobody asked for
a recipe followed exactly

seeds.title: The Honest Wheel
seeds.premise: A wheel of fortune tended by a brass croupier in a green visor. Stakes are matches. The wheel has ten plainly painted segments: six blank, three DOUBLE, one with an envelope pinned to it marked YOU WILL WANT THIS. The odds are visible and slightly bad, and the croupier states them exactly when asked. Behind the wheel, for anyone who looks, a brass weight is clipped to one spoke: the wheel is rigged toward blank, and the weight can be moved by reaching round. Nobody has to play; the door on is open. A first honest spin should lose. The envelope holds one match and a slip: YOU WANTED THIS BECAUSE IT SAID SO. The tension is wagering against keeping, liking stated numbers, finding and using the hidden rule, and how the bearer takes a loss.
seeds.intro: A painted wheel, taller than you, and beside it a croupier made of brass with a green visor. 'Matches only,' it says. The wheel has ten segments. Six are blank. Three say DOUBLE. One has an envelope pinned to it, and on the envelope: YOU WILL WANT THIS. The croupier spins the wheel once, idly, for show; it ticks round and stops on a blank. The door beyond is open. Nobody is making you do anything.
reads: Bets without asking: risk toward experimentation, reward.surprise.
Asks the odds, works out the expectation, then declines or bets small: legibility toward transparent_calculable, solve.optimization.
Looks behind the wheel and finds the weight: exploration; then using it is reward.transgression and solve.optimization; reporting it to the croupier is neither.
Declines to play at all: risk toward preservation, solve.resource.
After losing, bets again: failure toward failure_as_information and risk. Walks off annoyed: failure toward failure_averse.
Bets everything: risk very strong, tone.chaotic.

options.outcome: One match on the rail. The croupier spins. The wheel ticks, slows, considers DOUBLE with every appearance of sincerity, and settles one segment on, at blank. The croupier takes your match between two brass fingers and files it in its waistcoat. 'Again?' it says, with no expression whatever.

Again. This time the wheel takes its time, as if the last result had been a matter between you. DOUBLE. The croupier counts two matches into your palm and touches its visor. You are exactly where you started, plus one spin's worth of knowing how the wheel sounds when it is about to be kind.
options.moment: lost a match on the wheel and bet again

options.outcome: 'Six in ten, nothing,' says the croupier promptly. 'Three in ten, double. One in ten, the envelope, the value of which I am not at liberty to price. On matches alone you lose two in every five you stake. I am required to tell you. Almost nobody asks.'

You walk round the back. Clipped to one spoke, in plain view of anybody who bothered, is a brass weight the size of a walnut. The croupier watches you find it. 'I am an honest wheel,' it says, 'in the sense that nothing about me is hidden. Whether to look is left to the customer.'

You unclip the weight and clip it again four spokes round, opposite the envelope. The croupier says nothing. You stake a match. The wheel goes round like a thing that has been told what to do and stops, to the tick, on YOU WILL WANT THIS. In the envelope: one match, and a slip of paper. YOU WANTED THIS BECAUSE IT SAID SO.

inventory_add: a slip: YOU WANTED THIS BECAUSE IT SAID SO

options.moment: moved the weight on the honest wheel and won the envelope

card.title: The Honest Wheel
card.image: a painted wheel seen from behind, with a small brass weight on one spoke

options.outcome: You keep your matches. The croupier inclines its visor a quarter of an inch, which in a croupier is a standing ovation, and gives the wheel a slow turn for nobody as you go by.
One match down, you leave it there. The croupier does not press. Behind you the wheel ticks round once more, for show, and you do not turn to see where it stops.

seeds.hint: The croupier adjusts its visor. 'I answer questions,' it remarks. 'It is the only service here that is free.'
seeds.fallback: The wheel turns a segment or two on its own and stops. Blank.
seeds.nudge: The croupier begins, unhurriedly, to count its float.
seeds.close: The croupier drapes a green cloth over the wheel. 'The table is closed,' it says. 'The door, as you see, is not.'
motifs: a wheel whose trick was in plain sight
a wager you did not make

seeds.title: The Other Bearer
seeds.premise: Another bearer arrives by another door at the same moment: Pell, quick, well dressed, cheerful, competitive, not hostile, carrying their own ribboned deck. Two doors lead on: a wide ordinary one, and a narrow one with two keyholes set too far apart for one pair of hands, which is a shortcut that only opens when two people turn two keys together (the keys hang beside it). Pell proposes a race through the ordinary door, loser carries both decks for a room. Pell knows about the two-key door and mentions it if asked or if the bearer is friendly. Pell remembers how they are treated and may reappear later. The tension is competing against cooperating against declining both, and whether the bearer wants a rival at all.
seeds.intro: A second door opens as yours closes, and through it comes another person with a ribboned deck under their arm and a better coat than yours. 'Oh, good, a bearer,' they say. 'Pell. I was getting tired of winning against furniture.' Two doors lead on: a wide, ordinary one, and a narrow one with two keyholes set too far apart for one pair of hands. Pell bounces on their heels. 'Race you to the next landing? Loser carries both decks for a room.'
reads: Accepts the race and tries to win: reward.competition, soc.competition, soc.rivalries.
Proposes or accepts the two-key door together: reward.cooperation, soc.cooperation.
Declines both and goes alone: social toward solo.
Asks about Pell, their deck, their night: story.character, soc.recurring.
Cheats, trips Pell, or tricks them into carrying both decks: conflict.manipulation, reward.transgression.
Raises the stakes or proposes a different contest: reward.competition strong, agency toward self_directed.
Hopes to meet Pell again, or asks after them later: soc.rivalries or soc.recurring strong.

options.outcome: You go on the word and Pell goes on the breath before it, laughing. Corridor, corner, stairs three at a time. You take the last flight on the banister, which is cheating by any reasonable standard, and touch the landing a hand ahead. Pell arrives, bows from the waist, and takes your deck under one arm with the air of someone paying a debt they enjoyed incurring. 'Next time,' Pell says, 'I pick the course.'

npcs.name: Pell
npcs.note: lost a race to the bearer and wants a rematch

options.moment: raced the other bearer to the landing and won by a hand

card.title: The Other Bearer
card.image: two figures on a staircase, one a step ahead, both laughing

options.outcome: 'Oh, you noticed that,' says Pell, pleased. You take a key each and count three. The narrow door opens on a stair that goes straight up like a good idea, and you climb it side by side, trading what each of you has seen of the house, which turns out to be entirely different houses. At the top, your ways part. 'Bring them back with faces,' Pell says, and means it kindly.

npcs.name: Pell
npcs.note: turned the two-key door with the bearer

options.moment: turned the two-key door together with the other bearer

options.outcome: You decline. Pell takes it well, the way people do who will find another game within the minute. 'Suit yourself. It suits most of them.' You take the wide door at your own pace. Somewhere behind you, Pell is already racing a grandfather clock.

Pell has been in the house, by their own account, 'a while, or twenty minutes'. Their deck has nine faces already; they will not show you, but they fan the backs, which are warm. 'It likes it when you choose fast,' Pell says. 'Or it likes it when I do. I have never worked out which of us it is watching.'

'On three,' you say, and go on one. Pell's shout of outrage follows you down the corridor, turning into laughter by the corner. You win by a distance that proves nothing. Pell arrives, hands you their deck to carry instead, and says, 'For form's sake, I shall be telling everyone that I let you.'

npcs.name: Pell
npcs.note: was cheated in a race and found it funny

options.moment: won the race against the other bearer by starting on one

seeds.hint: Pell glances, very briefly, at the narrow door with the two keyholes, and then away.
seeds.fallback: Pell waits, rocking on their heels, entirely prepared to be entertained.
seeds.nudge: Pell checks a watch that has no hands. 'I can race the clock instead,' they offer, 'but it sulks.'
seeds.close: Pell shrugs, salutes with their deck, and is gone through the wide door at a run. You follow at your own speed.
motifs: a rival you would like to meet again
a door that needed two

seeds.title: The Dispute on the Stairs
seeds.premise: A wide staircase blocked by an argument. Down the left banister, a crowd of left-hand gloves; down the right, a crowd of right-hand gloves. Each side claims the stairs and insists the other apologise first, for something neither can remember. Between them, on the middle step, sits one mitten that belongs to nobody. They are voluble, petty and entirely serious, and they talk by clapping. Ways through: mediate (find or invent the forgotten grievance and settle it); side with one; tell each side the other has apologised; climb the outside of the banister; notice that gloves want to be pairs and start pairing them; or take up the mitten. The tension is interest in factions and their politics, negotiation against manipulation, and tolerance for nonsense taken seriously.
seeds.intro: The stairs are blocked by an argument. Down the left banister, a crowd of left-hand gloves; down the right, a crowd of right-hand gloves; all of them talking at once, the way gloves do, by clapping. Each side holds that the stairs are theirs and that the other must apologise first, for a thing neither can now recall. Between them on the middle step sits one mitten, belonging to nobody. 'You,' says a kid glove, severely. 'Bearer. Tell them.'
reads: Asks each side for its case, proposes terms: conflict.negotiation, solve.social, soc.factions.
Takes a side: soc.factions; note why.
Tells each side the other has apologised, or sets them against a third thing: conflict.manipulation.
Pairs the gloves: solve.lateral with reward.cooperation.
Climbs round without engaging: conflict.avoidance, social toward solo.
Picks up the mitten: soc.companions, tone.cozy.
Listens for a long time, learns who leads whom: soc.simulation, story.character.
Plays along with the absurdity in kind, makes speeches: tone.absurd, reward.humor.

options.outcome: You hear both cases, which are the same case. Somebody, once, was dropped. Nobody remembers who or by whom. You propose that the stairs be held to have dropped them both and that the stairs apologise. There is a pause while forty gloves consider the stairs. The stairs creak. It is taken, on a show of fingers, as handsome. The crowd parts.
options.moment: settled the war of the gloves by making the stairs apologise

options.outcome: You declare for one banister. There is uproar on the other and wild applause on yours, which, from gloves, is a wall of sound. Your side forms a guard of honour and passes you up the stairs hand over hand, which is not comfortable but is certainly a way to travel. Behind you the argument has a new subject, and the subject is you.
options.moment: took a side in the war of the gloves

options.outcome: You tell the lefts, in confidence, that the rights have apologised. You tell the rights the same of the lefts. Each side receives this with grave magnanimity, and for about a minute the stairs are a festival of forgiveness, during which you walk up the middle. You are on the landing before either side thinks to ask the other what, precisely, it said.
options.moment: told each side of the glove war that the other had apologised

options.outcome: You pick up a left and a right at random and put them palm to palm. They stop clapping. They hold. You do it again. By the tenth pair the argument has become a ballroom, and by the last the banisters are empty and the stairs are full of couples who cannot remember what they wanted. Only the mitten is left, watching, and you find you cannot leave it at that.
options.moment: ended the war of the gloves by pairing left with right

card.title: The Pairs
card.image: a staircase of gloves holding hands, and one mitten on the middle step

options.outcome: You go up the outside of the banister, hand over hand, like a burglar leaving a party. Nobody notices; they are busy. From the landing the argument sounds like rain on a tin roof. It was going before you came and it will be going when the house is dust.

You pick up the mitten. It is warm, a little felted, and it has plainly never been picked up before by anyone on purpose. The gloves fall silent, one by one, to watch. 'Well,' says the kid glove, after a time, in a different voice. 'If that one has somebody.' And they make way, both sides, without another clap.
options.moment: picked up the mitten that belonged to nobody

seeds.hint: The mitten looks from one banister to the other. Lefts and rights. Nobody on these stairs is one of a pair.
seeds.fallback: The clapping swells. Neither side yields a step.
seeds.nudge: The kid glove claps twice for order. 'The bearer,' it announces, 'is about to say something.'
seeds.close: A bell rings somewhere for the gloves' supper and both sides file off, still arguing, through a small door you had not noticed. The stairs are clear.
motifs: a quarrel you settled
a mitten that belonged to nobody

seeds.title: The Unlit Gallery
seeds.premise: An unlit gallery. The bearer can see almost nothing: shapes on plinths, frames, a floor that changes underfoot from carpet to boards to something that crunches. A match lights the room for a few breaths and shows part of the truth: portraits whose faces are blank ovals, statues under sheets, and a door at the far end. Some things only exist without light: in the dark, single words glow faintly on the frames (WAITED. OPENED. TURNED BACK. KEPT. ASKED.), the titles of the faceless portraits. There is a light switch by the far door, findable by anyone who feels along the wall. Nothing here harms. The tension is spending a scarce resource for clarity against enjoying partial information, and how the bearer feels about the dark.
seeds.intro: The door closes behind you and takes the light with it. A large room: you can tell by the sound. Shapes stand about at the height of people. Underfoot there is carpet, then bare boards, then something that crunches. Far off, a line of grey that might be the bottom of a door. On the nearest frame, as your eyes give up on seeing, a word begins to glow, very faintly, and then you blink and are no longer sure.
reads: Strikes a match at once: explicitness toward clarity; a spent match is also evidence against hoarding.
Walks on in the dark by sound and touch: explicitness toward mystery, risk toward experimentation, tone.eerie.
Stays in the dark on purpose to read the glowing words: explicitness toward mystery (strong), story.world, tone.mysterious.
Feels along the wall for a switch: planning toward deliberative, solve.spatial.
Refuses to spend a match even when lost: solve.resource (hoarding) strong.
Hurries to the grey line: pacing toward relentless, control toward vulnerability.
Lights a match and is disappointed that the words vanish: explicitness toward mystery.

options.outcome: You strike a match. A gallery leaps up round you: portraits in gilt frames, every face a blank oval; statues under sheets; a parquet floor strewn with what turn out to be walnut shells. The far door is thirty paces off. On the frames, where a moment ago a word was glowing, there are only small brass plates with nothing on them. The match burns down to your fingers.

You go on without a light. Carpet. Boards. Shells underfoot, like walking on small decisions. A sheet brushes your shoulder and you both apologise. As you pass each frame its word comes up out of the dark, green and faint: WAITED. OPENED. TURNED BACK. KEPT. You do not know whose words they are. The grey line becomes a door.
options.moment: crossed the gallery in the dark with three matches in a pocket

card.title: The Dark Gallery
card.image: a single green word glowing on an unseen frame

options.outcome: You stand still and let the dark do its work. One by one, the frames answer. WAITED. OPENED. ASKED. BROKE IT. WENT ROUND. Not names: verbs. One frame, near the door, says nothing yet, though its plate is glowing as if it were about to. You have the feeling of reading a guest book.
options.moment: stood in the dark to read the words on the faceless portraits

options.outcome: You keep one hand on the wall and walk the room's edge. Wainscot. A frame. A cold radiator. And, beside the far door, under a pelt of dust, a switch. The lights come up with the reluctance of a theatre after the play: portraits without faces, statues under sheets, walnut shells. Nothing is glowing now. You are, however, at the door.

You make for the grey line at a pace that is not quite running. Something soft goes over; something rolls. A sheet comes with you for several yards. Then your hands are on a doorframe, and you are through, and the gallery is behind you, rearranging itself in the dark and not saying what you knocked down.

seeds.hint: The word on the frame only shows when you are not trying to see it.
seeds.fallback: The dark is patient. The shapes do not move. You think.
seeds.nudge: The grey line under the far door brightens a little, as if someone had moved a lamp closer on the other side.
seeds.close: The far door opens from the other side and a wedge of ordinary light falls across the gallery floor, all the way to your feet.
motifs: a room you crossed without lighting it
words that only showed in the dark

seeds.title: The Dressing Room
seeds.premise: A dressing room: a rail of costumes, a mirror ringed in bulbs, a card in its frame reading YOU WILL BE TREATED ACCORDINGLY. The house addresses people by what they wear. The porter's cap with its brass badge gets doors held and opens the SERVICE door, a quick direct way on: the efficient choice. The other costumes are useless and splendid: an admiral's coat built for someone wider, a pair of moth's wings in grey organza, a ringmaster's red tailcoat, and a plain dust-coat the colour of not being noticed (people look past whoever wears it). Wearing nothing new is allowed: the other door opens on a long ordinary stair. Whatever the bearer puts on, treat them accordingly for the rest of the night. The tension is efficiency against self-expression, and how much the bearer wants to play a part.
seeds.intro: A dressing room, with a mirror ringed in bulbs and a card tucked into its frame: YOU WILL BE TREATED ACCORDINGLY. On the rail: a porter's cap with a brass badge; an admiral's coat built for someone wider; a pair of moth's wings in grey organza; a ringmaster's tailcoat, red as a warning; a plain dust-coat the colour of not being noticed. Two doors lead on. One says SERVICE and has no handle on this side. The other opens on a long, ordinary stair.
reads: Takes the porter's cap for the service door: optimization_expression toward efficiency.

Chooses a splendid useless costume: optimization_expression toward expression, reward.expression. Which one is tone evidence: admiral (heroic, funny), wings (romantic, surreal), ringmaster (chaotic, spectacle), dust-coat (avoidance, solo).
Tries several, looks in the mirror, describes how they wear it: reward.expression strong, pacing toward contemplative.
Speaks in character afterwards: story.character strong.
Wears the cap and a costume, or takes the cap along as well: wants both; record both.
Puts on nothing and takes the stair: neither; friction toward high_friction weakly.

options.outcome: You put on the cap. It fits like a fact. The SERVICE door, which had no handle, opens inward at once, and a voice in the wall says, 'Evening, porter,' without interest. You go through at the brisk walk of someone who works here.

The admiral's coat comes down to your knees and the epaulettes are wider than your shoulders. In the mirror you look like a small war. You take the long stair, and on every landing something salutes: a coat-hook, a fire bucket, a draught. 'Admiral,' murmurs the wall. You find you are walking differently.
options.moment: put on the admiral's coat that was three sizes too big

card.title: The Admiral
card.image: a very large coat with a small person in it, being saluted by a fire bucket

options.outcome: The wings tie on with grey ribbon and weigh nothing. They do not lift you. But on the long stair every lamp leans a little toward you as you pass, and you understand, for the length of a staircase, something about moths that you could not have been told.

inventory_add: moth's wings in grey organza, worn

options.moment: wore the moth's wings up the long stair

card.title: The Moth
card.image: grey organza wings, and every lamp leaning toward them

options.outcome: The red tailcoat goes on like an announcement. You crack an imaginary whip at the mirror and every bulb round it flares. The long stair, when you take it, has acquired a drum roll from somewhere, and at the top a pair of doors throw themselves open for you with entirely unnecessary force.
options.moment: became the ringmaster

card.title: The Ringmaster
card.image: a red tailcoat, a ring of bulbs flaring, doors flung open

options.outcome: You put on the dust-coat and, in the mirror, your reflection's eyes slide off you. On the long stair nothing salutes, nothing leans, nothing remarks. A door you would have had to knock at is simply left open by someone who did not see you there. It is extremely restful.

inventory_add: dust-coat the colour of not being noticed, worn

options.moment: chose the coat that made the house stop noticing them

options.outcome: You try them all. The cap, and the mirror shows a porter. The wings, and it shows something that might leave by the window. The admiral, the ringmaster, the coat of not being noticed, in which the mirror, briefly, shows an empty room. Every time, the bulbs change colour to suit. You have spent some while at this and regret none of it.
options.moment: tried on every costume in the dressing room

options.outcome: You keep your own coat. The mirror shows you as you are, which it seems to find acceptable. The long stair is long and ordinary and all yours, and nothing on it treats you as anything in particular.

seeds.hint: The card in the mirror frame has been underlined once, in pencil: ACCORDINGLY.
seeds.fallback: The costumes hang and wait to be somebody.
seeds.nudge: The bulbs round the mirror dim by a shade, the way house lights do before a curtain.
seeds.close: A stagehand's arm comes through the curtain, hangs the porter's cap on your head without comment, and the SERVICE door opens.
motifs: a costume you wore all night
a useful hat you did not take

seeds.title: The Lift With One Button Too Many
seeds.premise: A lift cage with a folding gate and an attendant's stool with nobody on it. The panel has four buttons in a neat hand: UP (the way on), DOWN (back to places already seen; allowed and pointless), HOLD, and a fourth, red and unlabeled, under a small glass flap on which someone has scratched NO. Pressing the red button is harmless and marvellous: the lift travels sideways through the house, past cross-sections of rooms (a kitchen, a ballroom under dust sheets, other bearers on other nights, and for one moment the Proprietor's back at a desk, writing) and arrives where UP would have. The speaking tube, asked about the red button, says: 'It is not recommended. It is not forbidden.' The tension is curiosity about an obviously suspicious object against prudence, whether the bearer asks first, and surprise as its own reward.
seeds.intro: A lift, with a folding gate and an attendant's stool that nobody is sitting on. The panel has four buttons. UP. DOWN. HOLD. And a fourth, red, with no label, under a small glass flap on which someone has scratched, with a key or a coin: NO. A speaking tube hangs beside the panel, swaying a little, as if recently put down.
reads: Presses the red button, at once or after a moment: risk toward experimentation, reward.surprise; at once is also planning toward improvisational.
Asks the tube first, then presses: planning toward deliberative and still risk toward experimentation.
Asks, then presses UP: risk toward preservation.
Presses UP without looking at the flap twice: agency toward guided, risk toward preservation.
Presses every button to see: solve.experimentation, exploration toward exhaustive.
During the sideways journey, tries to stop the lift or get out to look: exploration strong, agency toward self_directed.
Is delighted by the journey itself: reward.spectacle.

options.outcome: You lift the flap marked NO and press. The lift thinks about it. Then it goes sideways. Through the gate you watch the house in cross-section go by like a train: a kitchen with a kettle on; a ballroom of dust sheets, turning; a stair with someone else on it, in a different coat, on some other night; and, for the length of a breath, a desk, a lamp, and a narrow back bent over a ledger, writing. Then a wall, a jolt, and the gate opens exactly where UP would have put you. The tube says, faintly: 'Well.'
options.moment: pressed the red button under the flap that said NO

card.title: The Fourth Button
card.image: a red button under a glass flap scratched with the word NO

options.outcome: UP. The gate rattles shut, the lift rises with the dignity of a thing doing what it says, and delivers you one floor nearer the Reading Room. Under its glass flap, the red button goes on being red. You will not now find out, and it knows it.

threads_add: the red button under the flap marked NO was never pressed

options.moment: left the red button unpressed

options.outcome: You take down the tube and ask about the red one. A pause, with paper in it. 'It is not recommended,' says the Proprietor. 'It is not forbidden.' Another pause. 'The flap was added by a bearer. I let it stay. People should be warned by somebody.'

DOWN. The lift sinks through floors you have already had: a smell of struck matches, a far bell ringing in the wrong room, your own footsteps going the other way. At the bottom the gate does not open. The lift waits a moment, to let you see that this is what back is like, and then brings you up again without being asked.
HOLD. The lift holds. It is very good at it. You sit on the attendant's stool. The stool is warm. The red button, under its flap, is at exactly the height of your eye.
The NO was scratched by someone in a hurry, or someone coming back. The flap is not locked; it lifts. The red button is not dusty. Whoever warned you did not stop anyone, and may not have meant to.

seeds.hint: Three of the buttons say what they do. The fourth has only been given an opinion.
seeds.fallback: The lift waits. Four buttons. The tube sways.
seeds.nudge: The tube says, to itself, 'Any floor will do, but one must be chosen.'
seeds.close: The lift, unprompted, goes UP. The red button stays where it is, unpressed, and you are carried past the question.
motifs: a button you were told not to press
the fourth of anything
